You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - list [ref=e1623]:
            - listitem [ref=e1624]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1627] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-16"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.
            - listitem [ref=e1631]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1634] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-18"
                - text: ^
              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-23"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.
                - superscript [ref=e1641]:
                  - link "[20]" [ref=e1642] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197,_272Nardulli1992179-22"
            - listitem [ref=e1643]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1646] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-26"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1647]:
                - text: The 1796 presidential election was the first contested American presidential election and the only one in which a president and vice president were elected from opposing political parties. Federalist John Adams was elected president, and Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans was elected vice president.
                - superscript [ref=e1648]:
                  - link "[22]" [ref=e1649] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010274-25"

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

            - text: The

            - text: Under the

            - link "executive branch" [ref=e232] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e238]:
            - text: The first president,
            - link "George Washington" [ref=e239] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Washington
            - text: ", won a unanimous vote of the Electoral College."
            - superscript [ref=e240]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e241] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatuz2001xxii-4"
            - text: The incumbent president is
            - link "Donald Trump" [ref=e242] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Donald_Trump
            - text: ", who"
            - link "assumed office on January 20, 2025" [ref=e243] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e244]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e245] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHajela2024-5"
            - superscript [ref=e246]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e247] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreile2024-6"
            - text: Since the office was established in 1789, 45 men have served in 47 presidencies. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of
            - link "Grover Cleveland" [ref=e248] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Grover_Cleveland
            - text: (counted as the 22nd and 24th president) and Trump (counted as the 45th and 47th president).
            - superscript [ref=e249]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e250] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAP2024-7"
            - superscript [ref=e251]:
              - link "[8]" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchallerWilliams2003192-8"
          - paragraph [ref=e253]:
            - text: The presidency of
            - link "William Henry Harrison" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_Henry_Harrison
            - text: ", who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history."
            - superscript [ref=e255]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcHughMackowiak2014990–995-9"
            - link "Franklin D. Roosevelt" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt
            - text: served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms.
            - superscript [ref=e258]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkau1974246–275-10"
            - text: Since the ratification of the
            - link "Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
            - text: in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
            - superscript [ref=e261]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeabodyGant1999565-11"
          - paragraph [ref=e263]:
            - text: Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison,
            - link "Zachary Taylor" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Zachary_Taylor
            - text: ","
            - link "Warren G. Harding" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Warren_G._Harding
            - text: ", and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were"
            - link "assassinated" [ref=e266] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_assassination_attempts_and_plots
            - text: (
            - link "Abraham Lincoln" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Abraham_Lincoln
            - text: ","
            - link "James A. Garfield" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/James_A._Garfield
            - text: ","
            - link "William McKinley" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_McKinley
            - text: ", and"
            - link "John F. Kennedy" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_F._Kennedy
            - text: ), and one resigned (
            - link "Richard Nixon" [ref=e271] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Richard_Nixon
            - text: ", facing"
            - link "impeachment" [ref=e272] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Impeachment_process_against_Richard_Nixon
            - text: and removal from office).
            - superscript [ref=e273]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbbott2005627–644-12"
            - link "John Tyler" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_Tyler
            - text: was the first
            - link "vice president" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States
            - text: to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
            - superscript [ref=e277]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDinnerstein1962447–451-13"
          - paragraph [ref=e279]:
            - text: Throughout most of its history,
            - link "American politics" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_politics
            - text: has been dominated by
            - link "political parties" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States
            - text: . The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the
            - link "1st Congress" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1st_United_States_Congress
            - text: convened,
            - link "political factions" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_faction
            - text: began rallying around dominant
            - link "Washington administration" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Presidency_of_George_Washington
            - text: officials, such as
            - link "Alexander Hamilton" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alexander_Hamilton
            - text: and
            - link "Thomas Jefferson" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thomas_Jefferson
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e287]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197Nardulli1992179-14"
            - text: Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained
            - link "unaffiliated" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Independent_politician
            - text: with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.
            - superscript [ref=e290]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTELOC_(2)Jamison2014-15"

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.
            - listitem [ref=e1631]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1634] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-18"
                - text: ^
              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-23"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.
                - superscript [ref=e1641]:
                  - link "[20]" [ref=e1642] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197,_272Nardulli1992179-22"
            - listitem [ref=e1643]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1646] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-26"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1647]:
                - text: The 1796 presidential election was the first contested American presidential election and the only one in which a president and vice president were elected from opposing political parties. Federalist John Adams was elected president, and Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans was elected vice president.

                - text: Early during John Quincy Adams' term, the

                - text: John Tyler was elected vice president on the Whig Party ticket in 1840. His policy priorities as president soon proved to be opposed to most of the Whig agenda, and he was expelled from the party five months after assuming office.

                - text: When he ran for reelection in 1864, Republican Abraham Lincoln formed a bipartisan

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

            - text: (

          - paragraph [ref=e279]:
            - text: Throughout most of its history,
            - link "American politics" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_politics
            - text: has been dominated by
            - link "political parties" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States
            - text: . The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the
            - link "1st Congress" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: convened,
            - link "political factions" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: began rallying around dominant
            - link "Washington administration" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: officials, such as
            - link "Alexander Hamilton" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "Thomas Jefferson" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thomas_Jefferson
            - text: .

                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197Nardulli1992179-14"
            - text: Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained
            - link "unaffiliated" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.

              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.

              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.

                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEpstein2005318-3"
          - paragraph [ref=e238]:
            - text: The first president,
            - link "George Washington" [ref=e239] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Washington
            - text: ", won a unanimous vote of the Electoral College."
            - superscript [ref=e240]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e241] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatuz2001xxii-4"
            - text: The incumbent president is
            - link "Donald Trump" [ref=e242] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Donald_Trump
            - text: ", who"
            - link "assumed office on January 20, 2025" [ref=e243] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e244]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e245] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHajela2024-5"
            - superscript [ref=e246]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e247] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreile2024-6"
            - text: Since the office was established in 1789, 45 men have served in 47 presidencies. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of
            - link "Grover Cleveland" [ref=e248] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Grover_Cleveland
            - text: (counted as the 22nd and 24th president) and Trump (counted as the 45th and 47th president).
            - superscript [ref=e249]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e250] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAP2024-7"
            - superscript [ref=e251]:
              - link "[8]" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchallerWilliams2003192-8"
          - paragraph [ref=e253]:
            - text: The presidency of
            - link "William Henry Harrison" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_Henry_Harrison
            - text: ", who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history."
            - superscript [ref=e255]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcHughMackowiak2014990–995-9"
            - link "Franklin D. Roosevelt" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt
            - text: served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms.
            - superscript [ref=e258]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkau1974246–275-10"
            - text: Since the ratification of the
            - link "Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
            - text: in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
            - superscript [ref=e261]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeabodyGant1999565-11"
          - paragraph [ref=e263]:
            - text: Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison,
            - link "Zachary Taylor" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Zachary_Taylor
            - text: ","
            - link "Warren G. Harding" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Warren_G._Harding
            - text: ", and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were"
            - link "assassinated" [ref=e266] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_assassination_attempts_and_plots
            - text: (
            - link "Abraham Lincoln" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Abraham_Lincoln
            - text: ","
            - link "James A. Garfield" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/James_A._Garfield
            - text: ","
            - link "William McKinley" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_McKinley
            - text: ", and"
            - link "John F. Kennedy" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_F._Kennedy
            - text: ), and one resigned (
            - link "Richard Nixon" [ref=e271] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Richard_Nixon
            - text: ", facing"
            - link "impeachment" [ref=e272] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Impeachment_process_against_Richard_Nixon
            - text: and removal from office).
            - superscript [ref=e273]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbbott2005627–644-12"
            - link "John Tyler" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_Tyler
            - text: was the first
            - link "vice president" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States
            - text: to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
            - superscript [ref=e277]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDinnerstein1962447–451-13"
          - paragraph [ref=e279]:
            - text: Throughout most of its history,
            - link "American politics" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_politics
            - text: has been dominated by
            - link "political parties" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States
            - text: . The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the
            - link "1st Congress" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1st_United_States_Congress
            - text: convened,
            - link "political factions" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_faction
            - text: began rallying around dominant
            - link "Washington administration" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Presidency_of_George_Washington
            - text: officials, such as
            - link "Alexander Hamilton" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alexander_Hamilton
            - text: and
            - link "Thomas Jefferson" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thomas_Jefferson
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e287]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197Nardulli1992179-14"
            - text: Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained
            - link "unaffiliated" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Independent_politician
            - text: with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.
            - superscript [ref=e290]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTELOC_(2)Jamison2014-15"

              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.
            - listitem [ref=e1631]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1634] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-18"
                - text: ^
              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-23"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.
                - superscript [ref=e1641]:
                  - link "[20]" [ref=e1642] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197,_272Nardulli1992179-22"

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1647]:
                - text: The 1796 presidential election was the first contested American presidential election and the only one in which a president and vice president were elected from opposing political parties. Federalist John Adams was elected president, and Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans was elected vice president.

            - text: The

            - text: Under the

          - paragraph [ref=e238]:
            - text: The first president,
            - link "George Washington" [ref=e239] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Washington
            - text: ", won a unanimous vote of the Electoral College."
            - superscript [ref=e240]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e241] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatuz2001xxii-4"
            - text: The incumbent president is
            - link "Donald Trump" [ref=e242] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Donald_Trump
            - text: ", who"
            - link "assumed office on January 20, 2025" [ref=e243] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e244]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e245] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHajela2024-5"
            - superscript [ref=e246]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e247] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreile2024-6"
            - text: Since the office was established in 1789, 45 men have served in 47 presidencies. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of
            - link "Grover Cleveland" [ref=e248] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Grover_Cleveland
            - text: (counted as the 22nd and 24th president) and Trump (counted as the 45th and 47th president).
            - superscript [ref=e249]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e250] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAP2024-7"
            - superscript [ref=e251]:
              - link "[8]" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchallerWilliams2003192-8"
          - paragraph [ref=e253]:
            - text: The presidency of
            - link "William Henry Harrison" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_Henry_Harrison
            - text: ", who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history."
            - superscript [ref=e255]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcHughMackowiak2014990–995-9"
            - link "Franklin D. Roosevelt" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt
            - text: served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms.
            - superscript [ref=e258]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkau1974246–275-10"
            - text: Since the ratification of the
            - link "Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
            - text: in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
            - superscript [ref=e261]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeabodyGant1999565-11"
          - paragraph [ref=e263]:
            - text: Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison,
            - link "Zachary Taylor" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Zachary_Taylor
            - text: ","
            - link "Warren G. Harding" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Warren_G._Harding
            - text: ", and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were"
            - link "assassinated" [ref=e266] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_assassination_attempts_and_plots
            - text: (
            - link "Abraham Lincoln" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Abraham_Lincoln
            - text: ","
            - link "James A. Garfield" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/James_A._Garfield
            - text: ","
            - link "William McKinley" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_McKinley
            - text: ", and"
            - link "John F. Kennedy" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_F._Kennedy
            - text: ), and one resigned (
            - link "Richard Nixon" [ref=e271] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Richard_Nixon
            - text: ", facing"
            - link "impeachment" [ref=e272] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Impeachment_process_against_Richard_Nixon
            - text: and removal from office).
            - superscript [ref=e273]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbbott2005627–644-12"
            - link "John Tyler" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_Tyler
            - text: was the first
            - link "vice president" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States
            - text: to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
            - superscript [ref=e277]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDinnerstein1962447–451-13"
          - paragraph [ref=e279]:
            - text: Throughout most of its history,
            - link "American politics" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_politics
            - text: has been dominated by
            - link "political parties" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States
            - text: . The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the
            - link "1st Congress" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1st_United_States_Congress
            - text: convened,
            - link "political factions" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_faction
            - text: began rallying around dominant
            - link "Washington administration" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Presidency_of_George_Washington
            - text: officials, such as
            - link "Alexander Hamilton" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alexander_Hamilton
            - text: and
            - link "Thomas Jefferson" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thomas_Jefferson
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e287]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197Nardulli1992179-14"
            - text: Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained
            - link "unaffiliated" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Independent_politician
            - text: with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.
            - superscript [ref=e290]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.
            - listitem [ref=e1631]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1634] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-18"
                - text: ^
              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-23"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.
                - superscript [ref=e1641]:
                  - link "[20]" [ref=e1642] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197,_272Nardulli1992179-22"
            - listitem [ref=e1643]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1646] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-26"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1647]:
                - text: The 1796 presidential election was the first contested American presidential election and the only one in which a president and vice president were elected from opposing political parties. Federalist John Adams was elected president, and Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans was elected vice president.
                - superscript [ref=e1648]:

              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1704] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1705]:
                - text: Early during John Quincy Adams' term, the
                - link "Democratic-Republican Party" [ref=e1706] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party
                - text: dissolved; his allies in Congress and at the state level were referred to as "Adams' Men" during the Adams presidency. When
                - link "Andrew Jackson" [ref=e1707] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Andrew_Jackson
                - text: became president in 1829, this group became the "Anti-Jackson"
                - link "opposition" [ref=e1708] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Opposition_(politics)
                - text: ", and organized themselves as the"
                - link "National Republican Party" [ref=e1709] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: .

              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1715] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-36"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1716]:
                - text: John Calhoun, formerly a Democratic-Republican, founded the
                - link "Nullifier Party" [ref=e1717] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Nullifier_Party
                - text: in 1828 to oppose the
                - link "Tariff of 1828" [ref=e1718] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: and advance the cause of
                - link "states' rights" [ref=e1719] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/States%27_rights
                - text: ", but was brought on as Andrew Jackson's running mate in the 1828 presidential election in an effort to broaden the democratic coalition led by Jackson."

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1748]:
                - text: John Tyler was elected vice president on the Whig Party ticket in 1840. His policy priorities as president soon proved to be opposed to most of the Whig agenda, and he was expelled from the party five months after assuming office.
                - superscript [ref=e1749]:

                - superscript [ref=e1756]:

            - listitem [ref=e1758]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1761] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-ALincoln_55-0"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1762]:
                - text: When he ran for reelection in 1864, Republican Abraham Lincoln formed a bipartisan
                - link "electoral alliance" [ref=e1763] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: with
                - link "War Democrats" [ref=e1764] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: by selecting Democrat Andrew Johnson as his running mate, and running on the
                - link "National Union Party" [ref=e1765] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: ticket.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

## Summary
The president of the United States is the head of state and head of government of the United States, indirectly elected to a four-year term via the Electoral College. Under the U.S. Constitution, the officeholder leads the executive branch of the federal government and is the commander-in-chief of the United States Armed Forces.
The first president, George Washington, won a unanimous vote of the Electoral College. The incumbent president is Donald Trump, who assumed office on January 20, 2025. Since the office was established in 1789, 45 men have served in 47 presidencies. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of Grover Cleveland (counted as the 22nd and 24th president) and Trump (counted as the 45th and 47th president).
The presidency of William Henry Harrison, who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history. Franklin D. Roosevelt served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms. Since the ratification of the Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison, Zachary Taylor, Warren G. Harding, and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were assassinated (Abraham Lincoln, James A. Garfield, William McKinley, and John F. Kennedy), and one resigned (Richard Nixon, facing impeachment and removal from office). John Tyler was the first vice president to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
Throughout most of its history, American politics has been dominated by political parties. The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the 1st Congress convened, political factions began rallying around dominant Washington administration officials, such as Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained unaffiliated with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency.           - list [ref=e1623]:
            - listitem [ref=e1624]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1627] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-16"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.
            - listitem [ref=e1631]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1634] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-18"
                - text: ^
              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-23"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.
                - superscript [ref=e1641]:
                  - link "[20]" [ref=e1642] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197,_272Nardulli1992179-22"
            - listitem [ref=e1643]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1646] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-26"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1647]:
                - text: The 1796 presidential election was the first contested American presidential election and the only one in which a president and vice president were elected from opposing political parties. Federalist John Adams was elected president, and Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans was elected vice president.
                - superscript [ref=e1648]:
                  - link "[22]" [ref=e1649] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010274-25"

**Wikipedia:** [List of presidents of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States)

## Summary
The president of the United States is the head of state and head of government of the United States, indirectly elected to a four-year term via the Electoral College. Under the U.S. Constitution, the officeholder leads the executive branch of the federal government and is the commander-in-chief of the United States Armed Forces.
The first president, George Washington, won a unanimous vote of the Electoral College. The incumbent president is Donald Trump, who assumed office on January 20, 2025. Since the office was established in 1789, 45 men have served in 47 presidencies. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of Grover Cleveland (counted as the 22nd and 24th president) and Trump (counted as the 45th and 47th president).
The presidency of William Henry Harrison, who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history. Franklin D. Roosevelt served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms. Since the ratification of the Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison, Zachary Taylor, Warren G. Harding, and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were assassinated (Abraham Lincoln, James A. Garfield, William McKinley, and John F. Kennedy), and one resigned (Richard Nixon, facing impeachment and removal from office). John Tyler was the first vice president to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
Throughout most of its history, American politics has been dominated by political parties. The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the 1st Congress convened, political factions began rallying around dominant Washington administration officials, such as Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained unaffiliated with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.

          - paragraph [ref=e279]:
            - text: Throughout most of its history,
            - link "American politics" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_politics
            - text: has been dominated by
            - link "political parties" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States
            - text: . The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the
            - link "1st Congress" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1st_United_States_Congress
            - text: convened,
            - link "political factions" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_faction
            - text: began rallying around dominant
            - link "Washington administration" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Presidency_of_George_Washington
            - text: officials, such as
            - link "Alexander Hamilton" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alexander_Hamilton
            - text: and
            - link "Thomas Jefferson" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thomas_Jefferson
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e287]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197Nardulli1992179-14"
            - text: Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained
            - link "unaffiliated" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Independent_politician
            - text: with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.
            - superscript [ref=e290]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.

                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.

            - text: The

            - text: ","

            - link "term" [ref=e227] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: via the
            - link "Electoral College" [ref=e228] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/United_States_Electoral_College
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e229]:
              - link "[2]" [ref=e230] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShugart2004633–636-2"
            - text: Under the
            - link "U.S. Constitution" [ref=e231] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/U.S._Constitution
            - text: ", the officeholder leads the"
            - link "executive branch" [ref=e232] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "federal government" [ref=e233] [cursor=pointer]:

              - link "[3]" [ref=e237] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEpstein2005318-3"
          - paragraph [ref=e238]:
            - text: The first president,
            - link "George Washington" [ref=e239] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/George_Washington
            - text: ", won a unanimous vote of the Electoral College."
            - superscript [ref=e240]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e241] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatuz2001xxii-4"
            - text: The incumbent president is
            - link "Donald Trump" [ref=e242] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Donald_Trump
            - text: ", who"
            - link "assumed office on January 20, 2025" [ref=e243] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Second_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e244]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e245] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHajela2024-5"
            - superscript [ref=e246]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e247] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreile2024-6"
            - text: Since the office was established in 1789, 45 men have served in 47 presidencies. The discrepancy is due to the nonconsecutive terms of
            - link "Grover Cleveland" [ref=e248] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Grover_Cleveland
            - text: (counted as the 22nd and 24th president) and Trump (counted as the 45th and 47th president).
            - superscript [ref=e249]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e250] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAP2024-7"
            - superscript [ref=e251]:
              - link "[8]" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchallerWilliams2003192-8"
          - paragraph [ref=e253]:
            - text: The presidency of
            - link "William Henry Harrison" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_Henry_Harrison
            - text: ", who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history."
            - superscript [ref=e255]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcHughMackowiak2014990–995-9"
            - link "Franklin D. Roosevelt" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt
            - text: served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms.
            - superscript [ref=e258]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTESkau1974246–275-10"
            - text: Since the ratification of the
            - link "Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
            - text: in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
            - superscript [ref=e261]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e262] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPeabodyGant1999565-11"
          - paragraph [ref=e263]:
            - text: Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison,
            - link "Zachary Taylor" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Zachary_Taylor
            - text: ","
            - link "Warren G. Harding" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Warren_G._Harding
            - text: ", and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were"
            - link "assassinated" [ref=e266] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/List_of_United_States_presidential_assassination_attempts_and_plots
            - text: (
            - link "Abraham Lincoln" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Abraham_Lincoln
            - text: ","
            - link "James A. Garfield" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/James_A._Garfield
            - text: ","
            - link "William McKinley" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/William_McKinley
            - text: ", and"
            - link "John F. Kennedy" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_F._Kennedy
            - text: ), and one resigned (
            - link "Richard Nixon" [ref=e271] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Richard_Nixon
            - text: ", facing"
            - link "impeachment" [ref=e272] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Impeachment_process_against_Richard_Nixon
            - text: and removal from office).
            - superscript [ref=e273]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbbott2005627–644-12"
            - link "John Tyler" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/John_Tyler
            - text: was the first
            - link "vice president" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States
            - text: to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
            - superscript [ref=e277]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDinnerstein1962447–451-13"
          - paragraph [ref=e279]:
            - text: Throughout most of its history,
            - link "American politics" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/American_politics
            - text: has been dominated by
            - link "political parties" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_parties_in_the_United_States
            - text: . The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the
            - link "1st Congress" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/1st_United_States_Congress
            - text: convened,
            - link "political factions" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Political_faction
            - text: began rallying around dominant
            - link "Washington administration" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Presidency_of_George_Washington
            - text: officials, such as
            - link "Alexander Hamilton" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alexander_Hamilton
            - text: and
            - link "Thomas Jefferson" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Thomas_Jefferson
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e287]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197Nardulli1992179-14"
            - text: Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained
            - link "unaffiliated" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Independent_politician
            - text: with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. He remains the only U.S. president who never affiliated with a political party.
            - superscript [ref=e290]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:

              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1627] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-16"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1628]:
                - text: Presidents are numbered according to uninterrupted periods served by the same person. For example, George Washington served two consecutive terms and is counted as the first president, instead of the first and second, but Grover Cleveland and Donald Trump are counted twice because their two terms were not consecutive. A vice president who temporarily becomes
                - link "acting president" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Acting_President_of_the_United_States
                - text: under the
                - link "Twenty-fifth Amendment" [ref=e1630] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution
                - text: to the Constitution is not counted, because the president remains in office during such a period.
            - listitem [ref=e1631]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1634] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-18"
                - text: ^
              - text: Reflects the president's political party at the start of their presidency. Changes during their time in office are noted. Also reflects the vice president's political party unless otherwise noted beside the individual's name.
            - listitem [ref=e1635]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1638] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-23"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1639]:
                - text: Political parties had not been anticipated when the Constitution was drafted, nor did they exist at the time of the first presidential election in 1788–89. When they did develop, during Washington's first term, Adams joined the faction that became the
                - link "Federalist Party" [ref=e1640] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /wiki/Federalist_Party
                - text: . The elections of 1792 were the first ones in the United States that were contested on anything resembling a partisan basis.
                - superscript [ref=e1641]:
                  - link "[20]" [ref=e1642] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Guide_to_U.S._Elections''2010197,_272Nardulli1992179-22"
            - listitem [ref=e1643]:
              - link "Jump up" [ref=e1646] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_ref-26"
                - text: ^
              - generic [ref=e1647]:
                - text: The 1796 presidential election was the first contested American presidential election and the only one in which a president and vice president were elected from opposing political parties. Federalist John Adams was elected president, and Jefferson of the Democratic-Republicans was elected vice president.

              - generic [ref=e1705]:
                - text: Early during John Quincy Adams' term, the

                - text: John Calhoun, formerly a Democratic-Republican, founded the

                - link "Tariff of 1828" [ref=e1718] [cursor=pointer]:

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

## Summary
The president of the United States is the head of state and head of government of the United States, indirectly elected to a four-year term via the Electoral College. Under the U.S. Constitution, the officeholder leads the executive branch of the federal government and is the commander-in-chief of the United States Armed Forces.

The presidency of William Henry Harrison, who died 31 days after taking office in 1841, was the shortest in American history. Franklin D. Roosevelt served the longest, over twelve years, before dying early in his fourth term in 1945. He is the only U.S. president to have served more than two terms. Since the ratification of the Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution in 1951, no person may be elected president more than twice, and no one who has served more than two years of a term to which someone else was elected may be elected more than once.
Four presidents died in office of natural causes (William Henry Harrison, Zachary Taylor, Warren G. Harding, and Franklin D. Roosevelt), four were assassinated (Abraham Lincoln, James A. Garfield, William McKinley, and John F. Kennedy), and one resigned (Richard Nixon, facing impeachment and removal from office). John Tyler was the first vice president to assume the presidency during a presidential term, setting the precedent that a vice president who does so becomes the fully functioning president with a new, distinct administration.
Throughout most of its history, American politics has been dominated by political parties. The Constitution is silent on the issue of political parties, and at the time it came into force in 1789, no organized parties existed. Soon after the 1st Congress convened, political factions began rallying around dominant Washington administration officials, such as Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. Concerned about the capacity of political parties to destroy the fragile unity holding the nation together, Washington remained unaffiliated with any political faction or party throughout his eight-year presidency. **Wikipedia:** [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington)

## Summary
George Washington (February 22, 1732 [O.S. February 11, 1731] – December 14, 1799) was a Founding Father and the first president of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797. As commander of the Continental Army, Washington led Patriot forces to victory in the American Revolutionary War against the British Empire. He is commonly known as the Father of the Nation for his role in bringing about American independence.
Born in the Colony of Virginia, Washington became the commander of the Virginia Regiment during the French and Indian War (1754–1763). He was later elected to the Virginia House of Burgesses, and opposed the perceived oppression of the American colonists by the British Crown. When the American Revolutionary War against the British began in 1775, Washington was appointed commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. He directed a poorly organized and equipped force against disciplined British troops. Washington and his army achieved an early victory at the Siege of Boston in March 1776 but were forced to retreat from New York City in November. Washington crossed the Delaware River and won the battles of Trenton in late 1776 and of Princeton in early 1777, then lost the battles of Brandywine and of Germantown later that year. He faced criticism of his command, low troop morale, and a lack of provisions for his forces as the war continued. Ultimately Washington led a combined French and American force to a decisive victory over the British at Yorktown in 1781. In the resulting Treaty of Paris in 1783, the British acknowledged the sovereign independence of the United States. Washington then served as president of the Constitutional Convention in 1787, which drafted the current Constitution of the United States.
Washington was unanimously elected the first U.S. president by the Electoral College in 1788 and 1792. He implemented a strong, well-financed national government while remaining impartial in the fierce rivalry that emerged within his cabinet between Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton. During the French Revolution, he proclaimed a policy of neutrality while supporting the Jay Treaty with Britain. Washington set enduring precedents for the office of president, including republicanism, a peaceful transfer of power, the use of the title "Mr. President", and the two-term tradition. His 1796 farewell address became a preeminent statement on republicanism: Washington wrote about the importance of national unity and the dangers that regionalism, partisanship, and foreign influence pose to it. As a planter of tobacco and wheat at Mount Vernon, Washington owned many slaves. He began opposing slavery near the end of his life, and provided in his will for the eventual manumission of his slaves.
Washington's image is an icon of American culture and he has been extensively memorialized. His namesakes include the national capital and the State of Washington. In both popular and scholarly polls, he is consistently considered one of the greatest presidents in American history.
